data.title: End-to-End Test
data.tagline: An end-to-end test follows a complete system flow from a user's entry point to the final result.
data.learningOutcome: You can use one complete user task to judge whether a critical path really works from entry action to final visible result.
data.description: A browser can register, sign in, create a trip, and reach confirmation across pages, services, and data storage. This is evidence that the user journey works. Calling one API or checking one function is important but not end-to-end.

learning.assumes: You can complete a registration, purchase, or save by following page steps.
learning.outcome: You can use one complete user task to judge whether a critical path really works from entry action to final visible result.

distinctions.label: Integration test
distinctions.explanation: An End-to-End Test follows a complete user journey. An Integration Test can check only one connection, such as page to API or API to database.

explanation.title: Start at the user entry point
explanation.text: The test clicks, types, navigates, and reaches a final page, giving repeatable evidence for the real critical path. It fits registration, pre-payment confirmation, and content creation.

explanation.title: Keep journeys few and representative
explanation.text: Full journeys are slower and depend more on environments, so cover essential success and high-risk failure paths first. Unit and integration tests still locate detailed rules faster.

data.boundary: End-to-end testing is not clicking every test in a browser. It verifies a few critical user journeys; API and component checks can locate failures faster but cannot replace complete-flow evidence.

lessonPractice.title: Which best proves the end-to-end path “a user can complete a booking”?

options.label: In a browser, enter an itinerary, submit it, reopen the confirmation page, and verify it shows the saved itinerary
options.feedback: Correct. It goes from the user's entry action to the final visible result across needed systems.

options.label: Create the itinerary through the API, then check whether the matching record exists in the database
options.feedback: That verifies the service and data connection, but it does not start from the user's page actions or check the visible confirmation.

options.label: Fill and submit the itinerary in a browser, but only check whether the page navigates to confirmation
options.feedback: Navigation alone does not prove the itinerary was saved or that confirmation shows the submitted data.

data.agentPrompt: Add an E2E test for a trip booking: fill and save an itinerary in a browser, then reopen the confirmation page and verify that itinerary remains. After it passes, tell me which pages it visited and the final result it saw.
